newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks end up, but investors still wary.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks end up, but investors still wary.

text.p: Tokyo stocks ended slightly higher on Friday after a day of see-saw trade, but investors were still worried about further bouts of weakness after shares hit a 12-month low the day before.
The key Nikkei average of 225 leading shares veered between negative and positive territory before settling 77.46 points or 0.40 percent higher at 19,369.04.
Brokers said investors were still jittery about the health of the economy and the future course of stock prices, despite the mild correction.

"Noone thinks the Nikkei average had hit a floor when it tumbled on Thursday," one analyst at a second-tier brokerage said. "There are too many uncertainties, both fundamentally and externally, and it could fall again."
Turnover was fairly thin at 282 million shares, compared to 358 million on Thursday, as investors chose to stay away and wait for a clearer market direction to emerge.

The benchmark fell to its lowest level since early December 1995 on Thursday as investors, disappointed by the budget for fiscal 1997, took flight amid a lack of confidence over the future of the economy.
The budget includes a tax rise of nearly seven trillion yen ($60.8 billion) and a delay in a corporate tax cut, which the market fears could hinder the economy's fragile recovery.
"The weakness in the yen is also a worrying factor," said Haruo Nakaharu, a strategist at Toyo Securities.

The yen fell to a 44-month low against the dollar on Thursday, accelerating the stock sell-off. A weak yen cuts the value of Japanese stocks in dollar terms and makes them unattractive to foreign investors, who have been a driving force in the market.

"The 115 yen to the dollar level is within bounds, but if it falls further, to say 115.50 yen, while Tokyo is on holiday, the market could start the New Year with waves of selling by foreign investors," he said.
Japanese stock markets will be closed for New Year holidays from the end of Monday's half-day session, resuming on January 6.

Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Friday he was keeping a careful eye over movements in the stock market, and declined to comment on whether disappointment over the government's handling of the economy was behind the recent slide.
"Markets move according to market principles," he said.
He defended the government plans, saying the fiscal tightening was needed to offset previous tax cuts.
